speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: In Greek mythology in Homer’s “Odyssey”, after years of war and wandering, Odysseus faced one of his most perilous trials.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: To return home, he had to steer his ship through a narrow strait from which there is no turning back.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: On one side loomed Scylla, a six-headed monster perched upon the cliffs, each head striking with deadly precision to seize a sailor from the deck.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: On the other roared Charybdis, a vast whirlpool that swallowed the sea itself and dragged entire ships into the depths.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Sail too close to one and man would be taken one by one.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Drift to the other, the whole vessel will be lost.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: One danger was immediate and targeted; the other was systemic and consuming.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: So, he steadied his crew and held his course.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: He preserved his vessel, surviving by judgment, discipline and resolve.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: For small states like Singapore, this remains the eternal test – not to overpower giants but to navigate safely between them.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The post-Cold War order is giving way to sharper rivalry and deeper fragmentation.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The power of the law risks being replaced by the law of power.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: First, Mr Chairman, on the evolving global order and the defence of rules.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: As major powers compete across security, technology and trade, how will we preserve Singapore’s strategic space?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: When pressure mounts and blocs harden, how do we remain sovereign in decision, secure in defence and stable in prosperity?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Elsewhere, internal crises and external pressures test the principles of non-intervention and territorial integrity.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: For a small state, sovereignty is our lifeblood, our legitimacy, our survival.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: If might makes right, small states pay the highest price.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The question for the Minister is this: how will Singapore uphold a rules-based order consistently and credibly?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: How will we defend principle not only in word, but in deed – ensuring the same standards apply regardless of who breaches them?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We are also witnessing the erosion of multilateralism.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: For a trade-dependent nation, fragmentation hits our ports, our factories and our households.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: In this environment, what more must we do?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: What more can we do to strengthen high-quality trade agreements?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: How do we advance digital and green economy partnerships and push meaningful reform so that rules, not raw power, govern global commerce?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Second, Mr Chairman, on regional stability and conflict management.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Geopolitical tensions in the Asia Pacific remain acute.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: From the China-Japan row to flashpoints in the South China Sea, maritime incidents carry risks of miscalculation and escalation.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: How do we uphold freedom of navigation while avoiding binary alignments?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: And how do we reinforce the Association of Southeast Asia Nations (ASEAN) Centrality so that ASEAN remains the anchor for dialogue and peaceful dispute resolution?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: How do we contribute meaningfully to humanitarian relief and a credible path toward peace, without being drawn into the politics of others?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Third, Mr Chairman, on domestic resilience and shaping global norms.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Foreign policy no longer operates only beyond our shores.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: In an age of polarised narratives, it reaches into our information space and our social cohesion.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: How can we deepen public understanding that foreign policy shapes our food security, our energy resilience, our jobs and our safety abroad?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: How can we strengthen trust, unity and resilience at home?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: If we are to be steady abroad, we must be united at home.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Meanwhile, how can Singapore strengthen its role in protecting frontier domains?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: In cyber governance and artificial intelligence (AI), how can we help shape norms that are inclusive and safe?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: How are we strengthening cooperation on climate action and biodiversity to safeguard our seas, skies and digital space?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: And looking ahead, how will Singapore help write the rules for the new frontiers?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: How will we ensure that small states retain voice and agency in global rule-making?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Fourth, Mr Chairman, on bilateral relationships and strategic diversification.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: With the United States (US) and China, the challenge is enduring.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: How will we engage both constructively while remaining independent?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We must cooperate where we can and stand firm where we must.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: How do we maintain trust with both without becoming bound to either?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: How do we keep principled positions without becoming predictable instruments?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: How do we preserve strategic autonomy without drifting into isolation?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: With Malaysia, Indonesia and Brunei, our destinies are intertwined.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: How can we deepen connectivity and strengthen the ASEAN core so that ASEAN remains central in our region's stability?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Beyond our immediate neighbourhood, diversification is strategic necessity.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Chairman, I thank MFA for navigating in this complex external environment.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I have talked about the breakdown in the international world order in my speech for the Budget debate.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Today, I want to focus on how Singapore conducts foreign policy and the relationships it maintains, particularly in relation to free trade and security.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Therefore, the question is how Singapore should adapt to the evolving global environment in its conduct of foreign policy.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: First, we must be clear about what should not change.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: For a small state, like Singapore, international law ensures that our rights are protected.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Even when major powers disregard rules, it is not in our interest to do the same.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: We must remain consistent and ensure that when Singapore speaks on international issues, other countries recognise that Singapore is credible and its positions are consistent with its own conduct.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: When Singapore speaks on international issues, other countries recognise that its positions not based on expediency or convenience.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Economic relationships are increasingly shaped by strategic considerations.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: For example, as I have mentioned during the Budget debate, the US' position on the imposition of tariffs has been troubling.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: In this environment, Singapore's approach must be to remain open and connected.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This means that we must actively diversify our economic partnerships.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: We must deepen ties not only with major powers, but also across regions, such as Asia, the Middle East, Europe and other markets.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: It also means supporting high-quality trade agreements and looking into emerging areas beyond traditional commerce.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: By participating actively in shaping new economic rules, we can ensure that emerging standards and frameworks align with our interests and values.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: At the same time, of course, we must continue to strengthen our economic resilience at home, so that external shocks do not disproportionately affect Singapore's economic position.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Third, on security, it is also important that we maintain balanced and good relationships.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Our ties with the US and China, and other key partners each serve distinct and important interests.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: We should continue to engage all sides constructively, without being drawn into taking zero-sum positions.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This requires careful calibration as well as a clear articulation of our national interests, so that engagement with one partner does not come at the expense of another.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Singapore should continue to strengthen ASEAN-led platforms which promote dialogue and cooperation.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: In order to achieve these objectives, we must invest in diplomatic capability.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: To conduct foreign policy effectively, it is important that our diplomats have deep expertise.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Foreign policy today extends beyond traditional policy-making into domains, such as economics, climate and technology.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Our diplomats' capacity to operate across these intersections is crucial.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: MFA's work is especially important in these uncertain times.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I support the Ministry's work and its continued efforts and look forward to hearing about the Ministry's plans in response to the challenges we face.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Mr Chairman, as the global environment becomes more fragmented, supply chains are reorganising.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As a city-state, our resilience increasingly depends on trusted proximity and connectivity.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I believe that trust is the intangible infrastructure for us to continue punching above our diplomatic weight class in a fragmented global economy.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In line with my view of Singapore as a networked economy, Singapore's strength lies in becoming a key trusted node in connected regional systems – linking cities, industries and people.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Accordingly, I frame our foreign policy through three rings of strategic connectivity.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Recent engagements between Prime Minister Wong and Prime Minister Anwar reaffirm our commitment to managing complex issues constructively.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Likewise, the Singapore-Johor Riau corridor remains a natural growth platform.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Sumatra and the Riau Islands are in close proximity.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Few Singaporeans realise that the city of Medan is nearer to Singapore than to Jakarta.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We must therefore get Singaporeans to see opportunities beyond our shores.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Beyond our immediate borders, we must scale our trusted node status across ASEAN, Australia and New Zealand (ANZ), Northeast Asia, China and India.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The evolution of our overseas missions from mere representation to market paving and ecosystem building is critical.

speaker: Mr Victor Lye (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In this regard, I would be interested to know how MFA prioritises these neighbouring city and regional partnerships as platforms to help Singapore companies enter new markets and support Singaporeans seeking opportunities abroad.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Relying on traditional partners continues to be necessary but is no longer sufficient for Singapore to survive and thrive.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: We may become vulnerable if we over-depend on frameworks that no longer hold in this vulnerable era.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: While we often speak of ASEAN centrality, we must not let regional cooperation remain primarily a matter of diplomatic process, while global giants rewrite the rules.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Singapore must become a catalyst within ASEAN to coordinate our positions to exert collective bargaining power with middle and major powers.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: To do this, we must invest more in ASEAN's architecture.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This could include seconding MFA officers and having Singaporeans serve in leadership positions in the ASEAN secretariat.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This new era also requires small states to step up diplomacy.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: We cannot assume nations will respect us simply because of our economic success.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Our political leaders, diplomats and senior officials in all Ministries must cultivate deeper relationships with their counterparts in other countries.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The US-Singapore Free Trade Agreement was reportedly struck over a golf game in 2000 between then-Prime Minister Goh Chok Tong and President Bill Clinton.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Today, world leaders often communicate directly to strike deals.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Alexander Stubb, the President of Finland, which has a smaller population than Singapore, has shared how he is able to text message both President Donald Trump and Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Do our leaders maintain that same level of direct access to global decision makers?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Founding Prime Minister Lee Kuan Yew's early travels across Africa and Asia, built friendships that established support for Singapore and the global South for decades.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: He also built very strong personal relationships with leaders of global powers.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: We must build on this and not take this for granted.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: In response to my question if Singapore will be accepting the US' invitation on the Board of Peace, the Minister said Singapore is still assessing it.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: In the meantime, the Board has held its first meeting and it turns out, European nations that initially appeared to be staying out were there as observers.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Our neighbour, Indonesia, the world's largest Muslim majority nation, has also joined it.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Has Singapore made any decisions in this regard, including being at least an observer.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: To be clear, I am not calling for any commitment of funds or troops to the Board.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Establishing more resident missions in middle powers must take higher priority as we diversify our partnerships.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: For more than three decades after the Cold War, the world operated under a relatively stable framework underwritten by the leadership of the US.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Multilateral institutions such as the UN and WTO provided rules and processes.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Trade, technology and finance are increasingly instruments of geopolitical competition.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: As a small state in a strategic region, we must expect greater pressure as major powers compete.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: We uphold international law, freedom of navigation and ASEAN centrality.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Our trade is multiple times our gross domestic product (GDP).

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: If power politics prevails, small states suffer first.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: In that regard, I would like to hear MFA’s latest take on the evolving post-world order and what are the implications for Singapore?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Chairman, over the past year, the global geopolitical landscape has become increasingly tense, from conflicts in Europe and South America to rising frictions even within our region.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: International institutions such as the UN and the WTO are facing growing limitations in resolving disputes.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Increasingly, we see a world where power shapes outcomes and the principle of “might is right” is gaining ground.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: For a small and open country like Singapore, this is a sobering reality.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: We cannot take peace, stability, or prosperity for granted.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Our survival has always depended on foresight, resilience and above all, unity.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Against this backdrop, how will MFA position Singapore to navigate a more uncertain and fragmented world?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: How will MFA work together with MINDEF and other security agencies to strengthen our diplomatic, economic and defence resilience in the years ahead?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Equally important, how will the Government rally Singaporeans to stay united, vigilant and prepared?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: In a more dangerous world, our greatest strength is not just our military or our economy, it is the cohesion, trust and collective resolve of our people.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: Mr Chairman, technology has become a geopolitical tool to impact the geopolitical economy that we have.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: Right now, you can see the "IC war".

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: Not literally a war, but the barriers are being set up for technology transfer and also technology utilisation, trying to impede countries from moving from a higher level of technology capabilities.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: I think Prof Joseph Nair famously mentioned two things: power and soft power.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: But the question is how we utilise it for the benefits of Singapore and also countries surrounding us or even for the world.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: My observation is that technology, as we are practising right now, is on a lower level for foreign affairs.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: We set up technical assistance centres, we help our neighbouring countries and we offer scholarships.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: At a higher level, where we are in pioneering technologies such as quantum, such as AI.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: We typically leave it to either the industry or the research centres or the universities to implement, according to their relationships, maybe their complementary strengths.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: Would MFA consider technology as a strategic tool in our foreign policy that we upgrade and push as a soft power?

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: My proposal is whether we will upgrade our current technology directorate into an ambassador level or have a coherent way of putting all our technologies in Singapore, from the pioneering and not just on the pioneering capabilities, but also the absorptive capacity of certain countries, because different countries have different level of technology absorption capacity.

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: So, the training centres, will they be upgraded on a national scale rather than ad hoc basis?

speaker: Dr Neo Kok Beng (Nominated Member)
text: So, I am looking forward to a small strategic direction for our technology policy.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: A small, open economy, these shifts are not distant events for Singapore They have direct implications for our sovereignty, our economic resilience and the livelihood of our people.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: To protect Singapore’s independence as well as for Singapore to remain a trusted global hub for trade, we must understand the risks and respond decisively.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Where are the pressure points where their rivalry could squeeze our room to manoeuvre, and how are we protecting that precious independence of action that underpins our sovereignty?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: And importantly, how are we making sure Singapore is never pushed into taking sides – whether in technology standards, security cooperation, or trade – so that we can continue to act in the best interests of our people.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Because when supply chains are disrupted, it ultimately affects our jobs, cost of living, and the confidence businesses have to invest in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: And as global supply chains re-organise, how are we positioning Singapore as a trusted, stable hub so that businesses continue to choose Singapore, create good jobs and keep our economy strong?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: And just as importantly, how is MFA helping Singaporeans understand these risks in a clear, calm way, so people feel informed and prepared rather than anxious?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Mr Chairman, these questions reflect our shared responsibility to safeguard Singapore’s sovereignty and secure the future of our people in a more contested world.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: Chairman, Singaporeans have much to be grateful for and proud of.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: Singaporeans are privileged with visa-free access to 192 countries, signifying strong diplomatic ties, exceptional stability and good reputation internationally.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: The passport is but one outcome of what our foreign policy achieves.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: For us to remain and continue to shine as a red dot, our foreign policy has to be appreciated beyond our diplomatic call or in this House.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: It must also do so in our homes.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: Fellow Singaporeans must understand support and feel connected to it.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: There is a Malay saying, "tak kenal maka tak cinta".

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: If we do not know something, we cannot love it.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: Likewise, if Singaporeans "tak kenal", or do not know how and why our foreign policy matters in a complex world, then "Where is the love?", a famous chorus by Black Eyed Peas.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: Chairman, we are in an era where power is volatile.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: Institutions are under strain and geopolitical competition is intensifying, less constrained by shared rules.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: How do we safeguard our interests amid the weakening of the rules-based international order together?

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: Singapore's thrives on stability and a rules-based international system.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: Our economy, our security and our future, all closely tied to what happens beyond our shores.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: That is why strengthening domestic support and awareness of our foreign policy is so important.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: Singaporeans today are more globally aware than ever before.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: Many follow international developments closely and care deeply about humanitarian issues.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: Of late, we have seen how strongly Singaporeans here feel about Gaza, Ukraine and Sudan.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: Across communities, Singaporeans have shared the hurt and held the pain, each motivated to do their part, especially for women and children affected by the wars.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: Last year I was part of the Singapore delegation to Cairo, Jerusalem and Ramallah.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: Many Singaporeans reached out to share their concern.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: Some tried to unpack the complexities and many offered their support.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: Singapore has been unwavering in our humanitarian assistance to state solution, maintaining good relations and supporting the Palestinian Authority.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: Earlier this week, the Palestinian Authority's Minister for Finance and Planning, Dr Estephan Salameh, sat in this very House.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: I first met Dr Estephan in his office in Ramallah.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: As he was then, he remains hopeful of Singapore support and assistance.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: Singaporeans are too, and I am glad to learn that the Singapore Government has committed to that.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: Chairman, for decades, multilateral institutions such as the UN and ASEAN have provided platforms where law norms and collective voice help offset disparities in economic weight, military strength and political influence.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: We founded the Forum of Small States at the UN in 1992 to amplify collective voices of countries that do not possess the size or leverage of major powers.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: Small states must work together to avoid being marginalised in a system shaped by larger actors.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: Closer to home, ASEAN remains a cornerstone of Singapore's foreign policy.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: Our region's relative peace and stability did not happen by chance.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: It was built over decades of cooperation and trust.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: As geopolitical tensions increase globally, ASEAN's unity and central role will become even more important for the future of Southeast Asia.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: The Prime Minister also spoke about diversifying connections and levelling up engagement with us going regional, such as Latin Ameria, Africa and the Middle East.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: Building stronger ties with these middle powers will help Singapore remain relevant and connected in a changing world.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: And as we expand to new regions, how is MFA working across governments to ensure Singaporeans are equipped to engage them.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: One important step we can take is to prepare young people.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: Minister Chan Chun Sing earlier mentioned the importance of a Public Service building up global exposure and connections to understand the world well.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: Singapore should also take this move upstream and ramp up efforts to expose students to different cultures, languages and religions.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: Chairman, another Malay saying goes, "jauh perjalanan, luas permandangan", that is, the further you travel, the wider your view is.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: Foreign policy can sometimes feel abstract about strategy, geopolitics and international negotiations.

speaker: Ms Hazlina Abdul Halim (East Coast)
text: We must continue so Singapore will be bit and shine bright as a mighty red dot.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Chairman, Singaporeans are more interested and engaged in international affairs.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Greater awareness and interest in regional and global news is a strength we should support and nurture.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: But it also makes us more vulnerable to fake news, misinterpretations of events and developments.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: False narratives about Singapore or other countries can inflame sentiments and erode trust in our multiracial and religious community.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: What happens abroad can quickly reach our homes and our hearts, affecting our security, jobs and social cohesion.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: As a small, open and highly connected city‑state, we cannot afford for our foreign policy to be misunderstood or for our society to be divided by events far from our shores.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Such training can equip grassroots leaders with three things.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: First, a clear grasp of our foreign policy fundamentals, that we are guided by Singapore's long‑term national interests, international law and the need to maintain our autonomy and cohesion.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Second, practical skills to spot and counter disinformation: how to verify sources, recognise manipulation and respond calmly when residents share misleading or inflammatory content.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Third, scenario‑based exercises on sensitive issues, such as foreign conflicts involving race or religion, so that leaders can facilitate difficult conversations without letting emotions tear our social fabric.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Regular closed‑door briefings for key local opinion shapers can help ensure their public comments reflect an understanding of Singapore's interests and are not exploited by foreign actors.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Mr Chairman, navigating a world that has become more contested, more fragmented and ultimately more dangerous demands not just a capable foreign service, but a geopolitically literate citizenry behind it.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I say this, having served nearly seven years as a Singapore diplomat.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I know first-hand that our foreign policy is only as strong as our domestic understanding behind it.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Our diplomats are skilled but our foreign policy choices often involve navigating between imperfection options, not choosing between right and wrong.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And when difficult decisions must be made, whether to take positions that may temporarily strain relationships or navigate between competing interests, those choices are much harder to sustain without a public that understands why we make them.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Domestic geopolitical literacy is not a soft compliment to foreign policy.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is a foundation that makes hard choices possible.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But engagement and literacy are not the same thing, especially as several Members of this House have acknowledged, that in an era where geopolitical actors actively shape public narratives through digital channels, a dialogue session raises awareness.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Our students should graduate and enter the workforce with an understanding of how Singapore's prosperity depends on regional peace and open trade routes, why our stance on international law serves concrete national interests and how global shift and technology, climate and demography and more will reshape the world that they will inherit.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: A Singapore that understands the world that it lives in is a Singapore that can make hard choices and sustain them.

speaker: Ms Eileen Chong Pei Shan (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is the kind of resilience that no budget line can buy directly, but which only good education can build over time.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Mr Chair, recently, a resident approached me to ask if the Government will do a citizen consultation exercise on whether Singapore accept the invitation to join the US-initiated Board of Peace.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: She shared with me a poll on Yahoo, where 87% of respondents voted "no" and I believe that was her view as well.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I shared with her my view that while I am a big advocate for greater citizenship consultations in many areas, there are broader considerations for this.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: She replied that carrying out a public consultation was not about letting public opinion dictate our decisions, but to help ensure that the decision considers societal and cultural views and not just the Ministries involved doing work on its own.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In a world that is more divided, more volatile and more vocal than ever before and where attempts at foreign interference are rife, foreign policy can easily become a lightning rod for emotion.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Every citizen will have our own view on foreign policy, undoubtedly shaped by our cultural backgrounds and influences we are exposed to daily.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In this context, it is more important that we build up domestic support.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: First, anchor foreign policy in shared national principles.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Singaporeans will differ in views, but we must be united in valuing our shared principles.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: And if decisions are consistently framed around these principles, while there may disagreements or individual decisions, public will understand the logic behind them.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Second, be more transparent in how we explain our key decisions.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Not all negotiations can be conducted in the public square.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: But if the Government can explain the context, constraints and trade-offs more clearly after decisions are made, even if our citizens are not involved in the "how", they will better understand the "why", and their confidence will deepen.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Third, invest in education and strategic literacy and dedicate resources to schools, just like what Member Eileen Chong has just raised.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: A population that understands global economics, security realities and regional dynamics, will be much less susceptible to simplistic narratives.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We need calm, consistent voices that avoid inflaming sentiment, overtly or insidiously on both sides of this House, to set the tone for national discourse.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Mr Chair, building support for our foreign policy does not mean crowdsourcing strategy.

speaker: Mr Foo Cexiang (Tanjong Pagar)
text: It means building trust, strengthening understanding and reinforcing the values that have safeguarded Singapore's Independence and sovereignty for decades.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Some may ask whether it is time for us take a side.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: But doing so may not be in our national interest.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: The reality is that all countries need to work with both, which will remain consequential players regardless of how the international order changes.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Singapore's relevance to both major powers should not be taken for granted.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Why are both accounts important to us and how should Singapore work with both?

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Are there specific areas of cooperation that we are looking at?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Mr Chairman, Singapore's foreign policy has always been anchored in maintaining strong relations with all major powers while safeguarding our sovereignty and national interest.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Can MFA update us on how our relationships with the US and China have developed, and how we have continued to strengthen ties with both countries?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Even as we maintain positive relations with Beijing and Washington, the world is becoming increasingly bifurcated.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Partners like the European Union (EU), Japan and South Korea share our commitment to open trade, multilateral rules and a stable international order.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Deeper collaboration with these partners can help us expand economic opportunities, diversify our dependencies and uphold the global commons.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Can MFA share the initiatives Singapore is pursuing with such middle-power partners, along the geopolitical, trade and technology fronts?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: How are we working with like-minded countries to partially insulate Singapore from an increasingly fragmented world, while continuing to advance our national interests?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Small nations thrive when the rules-based order holds.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: I hope MFA can outline how Singapore intends to play an active role in strengthening that order along partners who share this conviction.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Mr Chairman, I will speak on Singapore's relations with the US and China, and our engagement with international organisations amid an evolving global order.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Singapore's foreign policy has long been grounded in a rules-based approach anchored in international law and multilateral cooperation.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: For a small, trade-dependent nation, respect for international law is not optional.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We are seeing signs of major powers recalibrating their roles within the traditional rules-based system.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The US has, at times, reduced engagement in certain international institutions and pursued new strategic groupings.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: China, meanwhile, has expanded its regional influence through initiatives, such as the Belt and Road Initiative and the Brazil, Russia, India, China and South Africa (BRICS) platforms.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: As new frameworks emerge, middle powers are reassessing their positions.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Singapore must be clear-eyed about this shift and consider how best to deploy our limited diplomatic resources across established institutions and emerging platforms.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Our approach should remain steady: engage with US and China constructively, uphold international law and safeguard our national interests.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: As an open economy reliant on trade and connectivity, a stable and predictable international order remains vital to our long-term resilience.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In a more fragmented environment, it is not about choosing sides.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It is about navigating competing frameworks with consistency, credibility and strategic discipline.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Chairman, in 2027, ASEAN will mark its 60th anniversary.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Over six decades, the region has moved from uncertainty to one that is more stable, connected and economically vibrant.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Major powers are competing more sharply and supply chains are reconfiguring.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In such an environment, ASEAN's unity becomes even more critical.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: When Southeast Asia is drawn into major-power rivalry, smaller states will have less strategic space to act independently.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Our shared interest must therefore be to keep ASEAN open, inclusive and cohesive, able to engage all partners while preserving its collective autonomy.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: At the same time, ASEAN must move with greater urgency on economic integration.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Greater alignment of digital rules and payment can enable our small and medium enterprises (SMEs) to operate more seamlessly across borders while regional energy cooperation can support our shared climate transition.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Singapore as Chair is well placed to advance meaningful progress in these areas.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In this regard, I seek two clarifications from the Minister.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In particular, how is Singapore supporting efforts to narrow digital capability gaps among member states so that integration benefits the region as a whole?

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: (In Mandarin):   Many entrepreneurs hope to expand their businesses overseas, but they worry about being unfamiliar with a foreign country and do not know where to start.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Currently, international situation is complex, competition between countries intense, supply chain adjusting, rules and standards are also changing everywhere.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Therefore, Singapore's diplomacy not only relates to national security and our international standing, but also directly affects the overseas development space for Singapore enterprises.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Although Singapore cannot influence power rivalry between big countries, it must maintain an open, stable, rule-based and predictable environment.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Only in this way can SMEs have the confidence to "go out, stand firm and go far".

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: As an ASEAN member, Singapore has consistently promoted regional economic integration and an open market.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Agreements like the Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership have created a larger, more dynamic market in Southeast Asia.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: I want to ask: do our enterprises really feel these macro achievements?

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: How are Singapore's relations with other ASEAN member states currently?

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: How can we work hand-in-hand with them through bilateral cooperation, as well as the ASEAN platform to achieve mutually beneficial and win-win outcomes?

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: In Europe, Singapore has deep relations with the EU, with the free trade agreement having been in effect for years, and green and digital cooperation also advancing.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Singapore's stability and law-abiding nature should be advantages for enterprises entering Europe.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: However, EU rules are complex and standards strict, creating barriers for SMEs.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: First, can diplomacy more proactively help SMEs "interpret rules"?

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: For example, overseas embassies, Government agencies and chambers of commerce could collaborate to provide regulatory information, market alerts and policy guidance, even creating an overseas investment guide.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Second, when expanding overseas networks, can we more strategically utilise Singapore's hub position in ASEAN?

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Let enterprises use Singapore as headquarters to expand into the ASEAN region; whilst maintaining Singapore-EU friendly relations, make Singapore a gateway for European enterprises entering Southeast Asia.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Transform "Singapore-ASEAN-EU" into a clear business platform with mutual reinforcement.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Enterprises "going out" is diplomacy and also becomes Singapore's diplomatic calling card.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: When Singapore enterprises build sustainable projects in ASEAN and provide digital solutions, engage in green finance cooperation in Europe, they are not just doing business, but also showcasing Singapore's standards, integrity and professionalism.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Corporate credibility strengthens national credibility, whilst national diplomacy expands corporate space.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Facing protectionism, will we more actively participate in regional rulemaking rather than passively adapting?

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Mr Chairman, diplomacy creates space for enterprises, enterprises create value overseas – both support each other.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Singapore may not be able to pursue scale advantages, but it can pursue value network advantages.

speaker: Mr Lee Hong Chuang (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: As long as we deepen integration with ASEAN, consolidate cooperation with the EU and let SMEs truly benefit, Singapore can expand its cooperation network in a complex environment and preserve flexible space for future development.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: Mr Chairman, ASEAN is important to Singapore because as neighbour states, we share many common interests and when we advocate and present ourselves as a regional bloc, can navigate as a stronger collective force.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: Amid the cloud of geopolitical uncertainty, ASEAN member states recognise the need for greater unity and integration.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: In this regard, ASEAN has taken considerable steps forward in the recent year.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: First, there has been more regional integration, especially in emerging areas such as the digital economy and sustainable energy.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: Second, ASEAN is a platform that can be leveraged to engage widely with countries around the world.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: The ASEAN Plus mechanisms and Dialogue Partnerships provide Singapore and ASEAN with regular touchpoints with major and middle powers.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: These include the East Asia Summit, which Singapore played a key role in establishing in 2005.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Chairman, in my work, I have witnessed how Singapore companies were able to operate confidently in ASEAN markets and collaborate on mutually beneficial platforms like the ASEAN Power Grid.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: This has been underpinned by diplomatic trust and strong government-to-government ties carefully nurtured over time through MFA's steady work.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: In today's fragmented world, ASEAN is more important than ever to Singapore.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: As a small state, our resilience and strategic relevance are strengthened when ASEAN remains cohesive and central.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Are there other regions besides ASEAN where we can replicate this cohesive diplomatic framework with?

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Personally, I believe we should institutionalise leadership networks so trust endures beyond personalities, strengthen ASEAN's crisis coordination for faster collective responses and reinforce ASEAN's credibility in wider regional and global platforms.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Diplomacy may not always be visible, but its dividends are real.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: In uncertain times, we must double down on steady principled engagement.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: For Singapore, that begins and remains anchored in ASEAN.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Mr Chairman, hon Member Hazlina spoke about the mighty red dot.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: At this point, I would like to make a book recommendation called "The Not So Little Red Dot" to everyone.

speaker: Ms Valerie Lee (Pasir Ris-Changi)
text: Not quite done with it yet, but so far, it has been a fascinating read of Singapore's 60 years of diplomacy journey.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa
text: We are witnessing tit-for-tat trade tariffs, export controls and increasingly troubling strategic posturing.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa
text: Countries in our region are understandably concerned, carefully evaluating their options in a more unsettled and uncertain landscape.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa
text: In this new multipolar world, ASEAN must navigate carefully and manage major power competition without becoming an arena for proxy rivalry.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa
text: Second, ASEAN must remain economically integrated and outward-looking.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa
text: Strengthening intra-ASEAN trade, supply chain connectivity and digital integration will reinforce our relevance.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa
text: Third, ASEAN must continue to anchor an inclusive regional architecture.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa
text: Even when major powers disagree, ASEAN can provide neutral convening space.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa
text: As a founding member of ASEAN, our strategic space is closely tied to ASEAN's cohesion and credibility.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa
text: A strong and united ASEAN enlarges Singapore's diplomatic and economic space.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa
text: Under this setting, can I ask MFA how can ASEAN ensure continued relevance and what are the implications for Singapore?

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Patrick Tay, you may take your two cuts together.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: ASEAN has long been described as a core strategic asset for Singapore.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Could MFA elaborate on how it is strengthening ASEAN's role as a stable regional framework, one that amplifies the collective voice of its members and anchors Southeast Asia in an open, inclusive and rules-based order?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: In particular, how is the Ministry advancing economic integration, supply chain resilience and ASEAN centrality in a more fragmented global system?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: On regional peace and stability, how is MFA working with our neighbours to reinforce ASEAN-led mechanisms, manage differences through dialogue and uphold international law, especially in areas of growing strategic tension?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: What concrete steps are being taken to advance cooperation in the digital economy, green transition and human capital development so that ASEAN remains competitive and resilient?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: I would be grateful if the Ministry could address how these efforts together safeguard Singapore's long-term interests and regional stability.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: On relations with Malaysia, Indonesia and ASEAN neighbours, Chairman, I would like to ask MFA how Singapore is stepping up engagement with our immediate neighbours, particularly Malaysia and Indonesia, in a more uncertain and competitive global environment.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: First, beyond our well-established bilateral frameworks, how is MFA refreshing and prioritising engagement to ensure these relationships remain strategically relevant and responsive to new challenges?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Second, could MFA elaborate on what new or emerging domains it is actively developing with our neighbours?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: In particular, how is MFA advancing cooperation in areas, such as the digital economy, renewable energy, sustainability and supply chain resilience, and how are these being translated into concrete, practical projects?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Third, how is MFA strengthening engagement at the sub-national level?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: What role do partnerships with Malaysian states and Indonesian provinces play in Singapore's broader regional strategy, and how does MFA ensure these ground-up collaborations deliver tangible outcomes?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: I would be grateful if the Ministry could address how these efforts collectively strengthen Singapore's security, economic resilience and strategic space.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nee Soon)
text: Chairman, as Members have already shared, the world is indeed more tumultuous and uncertain.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nee Soon)
text: Several flashpoints around the world – Ukraine-Russia, Israel-Palestine, US-China – continue to remind us that even in a world with largely ample global resource to solve crises, matters that transcend boundaries have not been so easy to find a resolution to and clear long-term solutions continue to elude us.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nee Soon)
text: Because when the rubber hits the road, sovereign nations look out for their interest first.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nee Soon)
text: Such a message is not lost on us as a small country that has to manoeuvre through headwinds where big players muscle in and make every attempt to influence.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nee Soon)
text: In fact, of late, any effort to converge towards multilateralism appears to swim against a very tough tide.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nee Soon)
text: Yet the plan is met with much cynicism.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nee Soon)
text: Save for the US, no other permanent member of the UN Security Council has come on board this plan.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nee Soon)
text: While the ceasefire in Gaza has held to some extent, the situation remains dire and fragile.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nee Soon)
text: Israel has recently made moves to tighten control over the West Bank and Hamas continues to be tentative in disarmament.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nee Soon)
text: In the meantime, while outwardly, armed conflict appears to have been dialed down, ordinary Palestinians continue to suffer in the middle of this impasse.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nee Soon)
text: Singaporeans continue to be deeply concerned about the humanitarian crisis for which a longer-term resolution still remains unclear.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nee Soon)
text: Indeed, how we manage this crisis has parallel lessons for us in how we navigate our foreign diplomacy and relations moving forward.

speaker: Dr Syed Harun Alhabsyi (Nee Soon)
text: How we balance our existing relationships with countries we have traditionally regarded as friends, how we push against flagrant breaches of international law by countries, how we maintain our position as a principled, trusted partner in the global stage and ultimately, how we look out for our national interests for Singapore and Singaporeans.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Mr Chairman, Sir, Singapore has long excelled in government-to-government diplomacy.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Our bilateral partnerships and multilateral engagement remain strong foundations of our foreign policy.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: But today's geopolitical environment requires us to go one level deeper.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Resilience is no longer built only through state relationships.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: It is built through networks of people, institutions and shared capabilities.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Middle powers, such as South Korea, Australia, the Nordic states, the United Arab Emirates (UAE) and our ASEAN neighbours, we face similar challenges – navigating major power competition, sustaining open economies, managing ageing populations, strengthening social cohesion and fighting low total fertility rates.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: These shared realities create natural grounds for deeper partnership.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: After all, there is something special about bonds forged through shared challenges.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Yet structured platforms for sustained collaboration between Singaporeans and our counterparts in these countries remain limited.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: I would therefore seek the Minister's view on three areas.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Second, how we might facilitate longer term institutional partnerships connecting SMEs, research institutions, healthcare systems and civic organisations.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: And third, whether MFA could expand Track 1.5 dialogues at people-to-people platforms to include younger professionals and community leaders from diverse sectors.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Mr Chairman, Sir, in an increasingly multipolar world, influence is not defined by size but by the strength of our networks.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira
text: Chairman, with the shifting supply chains and new growth poles, emerging regions, such as Africa, Latin America and the Middle East, will be critical to Singapore's long‑term resilience.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira
text: Our Government can and must play a bigger role in helping Singaporeans venture confidently into these frontiers, gaining a deep understanding of these countries and establishing friendships with their peoples.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira
text: Our new and existing Missions in emerging regions should be resourced not just for diplomatic presence or administrative protocol, but as active economic enablers, working in tandem with the Ministry of Trade and Industry in mapping sectoral opportunities, curating pipelines of projects and matching them with Singapore companies, workers and researchers.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira
text: We must give Singaporeans the assurance that when they go farther, they are not going alone.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira
text: We should build on this by investing further in consular readiness in emerging regions, widening public awareness of eRegistration and the 24-hour MFA Duty Office hotline and travel advisories.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira
text: We should nurture a new generation of "frontier‑ready" Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira
text: In many countries, strong relationships are the most important ingredients for successful outcomes.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira
text: Singaporeans must be empowered to form these relationships between peoples at the business and at the political level.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira
text: This is the reality of how the world works that we cannot change and it is also something that AI is not able to easily replace.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira
text: We can expand scholarships, internships and mid‑career attachments in emerging regions, especially in sectors where our capabilities align with their needs, including sustainability and digital services.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira
text: When young Singaporeans live, study and work in these places, they build language skills, networks and a feel for the ground that no brochure or academic course can replicate.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira
text: I hope to see more plans and initiatives that help to position Singapore as the indispensable hub for Latin American countries looking to enter the ASEAN market and with greater participation opportunities available to Singapore.

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: Chairman, in a more contested and volatile world, small states cannot afford to stand alone.

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: We must build coalitions not only through trade and security, but through development partnerships.

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: Singapore's credibility comes from experience: building trusted institutions, strengthening governance, managing public finance with discipline and developing talent and urban systems under constraint.

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: In this changed world, success cannot mean Singapore simply running far ahead.

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: We have both an obligation and a strategic interest in mutual knowledge sharing with fellow small states, middle powers and our regional neighbours.

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: How are we strengthening sustained capacity-building platforms – talent exchanges, not just in education and work but in the sports and arts as well; institutional partnerships and governance collaboration – so that we build enduring networks of trust, not one-off engagements?

speaker: Assoc Prof Kenneth Goh (Nominated Member)
text: In a fragmented world, influence is built not by size, but through sharing our capabilities together.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong
text: Chairman, as more Singaporeans study, work and travel abroad, many may not realise that wherever our citizens go, Singapore quietly maintains a constant watch over their safety.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong
text: For example, Australia and Canada provide reciprocal assistance to each other's citizens in locations where one country may not have a diplomatic presence, allowing travellers to access basic emergency to help locally.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Mr Chairman, on behalf of my colleagues, I first thank all Members for their ideas, their suggestions.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: And I must say, again, this year, I think I can claim bi-partisan support for MFA.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: In the last 60-plus years of Singapore's Independence, actually, we evolved exquisitely to take full advantage of this global system.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: And we benefited from Pax Americana, from China's reform and opening, from the rise of middle powers and the progressive integration of ASEAN.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: In fact, Singapore thrives as a global metropolis in an age of globalisation.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: The first brutal hard truth is that if that period has ended, we cannot simply presume that we just carry on as per normal, somehow magically, things will fall into place.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: It is also worth asking ourselves why and how that benign era of globalisation has ended.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Actually, foreign policy begins at home and this applies in understanding what is happening now on the global stage.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: In many countries, there has been a populist backlash.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Globalisation has created wealth, but it is also blamed for accentuating fault lines, for increasing inequality, for middle-class stagnation, for the loss of jobs, for growing despair and deep polarisation in many societies.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: This domestic dysfunction has now projected itself onto the global stage and you will see that this has undermined the support for the international order.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: So, I completely agree with Mr Yip Hon Weng, Mr Vikram Nair, Mr Liang Eng Hwa and Gerald Giam.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: The Greek historian Thucydides wrote, “The strong do what they can and the weak suffer what they must”.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Today, the Great Powers flex their military and economic power more readily than ever before in pursuit of their interests more narrowly defined.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: And to be frank, with less pretence of legal or moral justification for their actions.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Where there was once economic integration, there is now fragmentation and weaponisation of interdependence and dependence.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: We are now in a world where international relations are no longer driven primarily by rules or by attempts to achieve consensus.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Actually, the Great Powers have always been selective when applying the rule of law to themselves.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: But now, they feel even less need to engage in hypocrisy.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: It is all about how raw power and how that raw power asymmetry can be exploited.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: And so, this is a more dangerous world for small countries, because small countries do not have the strategic heft to buffer ourselves from turbulence.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: For Singapore, a tiny city-state, the shoals are even more treacherous.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Let us pause for a moment to consider what our options are.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: First option: despair, give up, surrender to our fates.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: I think the answer must be no, because that is not who we are.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: This is not who we were in 1965 when in fact, a newly independent Singapore faced even longer odds with less resources.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Second option: choose one dominant power and seek protection under its wing.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: This would undermine our sovereignty, our independence, and in effect, make us a vassal state.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Singapore should not and does not need to do this.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: And after all, Singapore has never expected anyone else to come to our defence.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Yes, we may be small, but we are a sovereign and independent country.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: We are a trusted global hub and an assiduous bridge builder.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: We want to make common cause with all states that are willing to engage us.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: We build regional and global networks that support dialogue, openness and inclusion.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: We want to be useful but not made use of.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: We are successful because of our domestic unity, our economic relevance and vitality, and our defence capabilities.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Therefore, we may be small, but we have agency, we have resilience and we have the resources and the will to back this up.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Mr Yip Hon Weng asked how Singapore will defend our principles not just in words, but also in deed.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Singapore's foreign policy has always rested on two pillars.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Mr Rajaratnam described the first pillar as “the theology of foreign policy”.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: That means, the world that we hope to have, a world that hopefully was based on principles of fairness, sovereign equality and international rules.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: There is a deep vein of realism in the way we view the world and the way we operate.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: This is what Mr Rajaratnam termed “the practice of foreign policy”.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: We have always understood that size and power matter in foreign relations.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: We never want to become so cynical that no one will trust us.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: But we also do not want to be so naïve that we will get taken advantage of by everyone.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: We need to assess objectively our national interests based on our unique circumstances as a tiny multiracial city-state in the heart of Southeast Asia.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: So, the next set of questions: what are our national interests?

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Energy, food, water – and you can add to that list.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: In such a tumultuous world, the point I am making today is that we are going to face more strategic dilemmas and difficult choices.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Because, for instance, our interests are not always going to be aligned with the Great Powers, all the middle powers, or our immediate neighbours.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: On some issues, and this is the key point that we are making today, on some issues, we will have to say “no”, to say "no" courteously, respectfully and constructively.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: But nevertheless, we stand firm and say "no".

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: This is not about choosing sides but about upholding principles and a careful assessment of Singapore's long-term national interests.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: I have been in this post long enough to tell you that pressure has been and will be brought to bear on us.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: There will always be attempts to weaken our will and to divide us domestically.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: I will also state that sometimes we will pay a price for staking our position but I am hoping that this House and the citizens beyond will agree that we must retain this ability to say "no" when we have to and that if we ever lose that ability to say "no", then that is the day that Singapore loses its relevance, indeed, our independence.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Let us provide some examples so it is not just words.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: We have consistently called out violations of international law.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: To us, that was a clear violation of international law and the principles of the UN Charter.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: More recently, we also did so in relation to the US actions in Venezuela.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: And we took these positions because a world based on "might is right" is a world that is more dangerous for Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: We spoke out about the need to preserve a rules based trading system, including the principle of most favoured nation in the WTO.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: We expressed categorically our disappointment with the US tariffs that violate this principle, because trade is our lifeblood.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Trade is more than three times Singapore's GDP.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Jobs, investments and living standards depend on our predictable access to external markets.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: We also took clear positions on the Israel Gaza conflict.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: We condemn the attacks that occurred on 7 October 2023 on Israel.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: We affirm that every state has a right of self defence.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: However, in exercising this right, countries must abide by international law, including international humanitarian law, and we have clearly stated that Israel's military response has breached international humanitarian law.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: I agree with Mr Yip Hon Weng on the need for both moral clarity and diplomatic effectiveness, although I would add that we must not try to reduce foreign relations into a morality play.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: I think you will be hard pressed to find occasions when the Prime Minister or I will ever refer to anyone, any other leader or any other country as evil or saint.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: That is not the way things work in real life.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: And more than just money, that there are Singaporeans lining up to volunteer their services, their professional services to help on the ground.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: To answer Mr Gerald Giam, we are still assessing the invitation from the US to formally join the Board of Peace, but in the meantime, we will explore initiatives, including those that were recently announced at the inaugural meeting of the Board of Peace on 19 February 2026.

speaker: The Minister for Foreign Affairs (Dr Vivian Balakrishnan)
text: Singapore will continue to play a constructive role in the pursuit of peace and reconstruction in Gaza, and on Palestine, the larger question.
